title: Skeletal muscle: contraction and major muscles
note: A muscle fiber contracts when acetylcholine triggers an action potential, calcium is released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, and calcium binding to troponin moves tropomyosin off actin so myosin can pull. A muscle's action follows from its insertion moving toward its origin.

read.title: From nerve signal to pull
text: A skeletal muscle fiber does nothing until a motor neuron tells it to. At the neuromuscular junction, the neuron releases acetylcholine, which binds receptors on the motor end-plate and starts an action potential in the sarcolemma. T-tubules carry that signal deep into the fiber, next to the sarcoplasmic reticulum, which responds by releasing stored calcium.

In a resting fiber, tropomyosin lies across actin and blocks the sites where myosin would bind. Calcium changes that. It binds troponin, which shifts tropomyosin aside and exposes the binding sites. Myosin heads, already cocked with energy from splitting ATP, attach to actin and pivot in a power stroke that slides the thin filaments toward the center of the sarcomere. A new ATP binding to each head releases it so it can re-cock and pull again.

As this cycle repeats, the Z-discs draw closer and the sarcomere shortens, although the filaments themselves keep their length. That is why the A band, which spans the thick filaments, stays the same width.
Relaxation is active too. When nerve signals stop, ATP-driven pumps return calcium to the sarcoplasmic reticulum, tropomyosin covers actin again, and the fiber relaxes.

q.q: What exposes the myosin-binding sites on actin?
What does a new ATP do for a myosin head after the power stroke?
o: Pumps calcium out of the cell

q.q: Why does the A band keep its width during contraction?
o: The filaments slide but do not shorten
